item.title: Invertase Substrate Specificity and Reaction Rate
item.stimulus:
Invertase is an enzyme produced by yeast. It catalyzes the hydrolysis of the disaccharide sucrose into glucose and fructose. A student wants to know whether invertase can also hydrolyze two other glucose-containing disaccharides, lactose and maltose. Hydrolysis of any of these three disaccharides releases glucose, so the student uses glucose production as a measure of enzyme activity.

The student sets up four tubes. Each tube contains 5 mL of pH 4.5 buffer and 10 mmol/L of one disaccharide. Invertase solution (1 mL) is added to Tubes 1, 3 and 4. Tube 2 receives 1 mL of buffer instead of enzyme. All tubes are kept at 37 °C. No tube contains glucose at the start. After 10 minutes, the amount of glucose in each tube is measured.

Tube | Disaccharide | Invertase added | Glucose after 10 min (µmol)
1 | Sucrose | Yes | 24.0
2 | Sucrose | No | 0.2
3 | Lactose | Yes | 0.2
4 | Maltose | Yes | 0.3
item.model_answer:
(a) The independent variable is the type of disaccharide used as substrate (sucrose, lactose or maltose). The dependent variable is the amount of glucose produced after 10 minutes.

(b) Tube 2 is a negative control containing sucrose but no invertase. It produced only 0.2 µmol of glucose, showing that sucrose breaks down very little on its own under these conditions. Therefore the 24.0 µmol of glucose in Tube 1 can be attributed to invertase activity rather than to spontaneous breakdown of sucrose.

(c) Tube 1 rate = 24.0 µmol ÷ 10 min = 2.4 µmol/min. Tube 2 rate = 0.2 µmol ÷ 10 min = 0.02 µmol/min. 2.4 ÷ 0.02 = 120, so the reaction with invertase is 120 times faster. Invertase is a protein catalyst that lowers the activation energy of sucrose hydrolysis. With a lower energy barrier, many more sucrose molecules react per minute, so glucose is produced much faster in Tube 1 than in Tube 2, where the reaction must overcome the higher uncatalyzed activation energy.

(d) Invertase does not hydrolyze lactose or maltose. Tubes 3 and 4 produced only 0.2 and 0.3 µmol of glucose, about the same as the no-enzyme control and far less than the 24.0 µmol from sucrose. According to the enzyme-substrate complex model, a substrate's shape and charge must be compatible with the enzyme's active site. Lactose and maltose differ in shape from sucrose, so they do not fit invertase's active site, no enzyme-substrate complex forms, and the activation energy for their hydrolysis is not lowered.

item.title: Substrate Specificity of a Yeast Sucrase Enzyme
item.stimulus:
Yeast cells produce sucrase, an enzyme that catalyzes the hydrolysis of the disaccharide sucrose into glucose and fructose. Sucrase is a protein. Other disaccharides, such as maltose (glucose + glucose) and lactose (glucose + galactose), also release glucose if hydrolyzed.

A student set up four test tubes. Each tube held 5 mL of a 2% disaccharide solution in buffer at pH 7 and was kept at 25 °C. Then 1 mL of purified sucrase solution or 1 mL of buffer alone was added. After 10 minutes, the student measured the mass of free glucose in each tube.

Tube | Disaccharide | Addition | Glucose after 10 min (mg)
1 | Sucrose | Sucrase | 4.8
2 | Maltose | Sucrase | 0.1
3 | Lactose | Sucrase | 0.1
4 | Sucrose | Buffer only | 0.1
item.model_answer:
(a) The independent variable is the type of disaccharide (substrate) given to sucrase: sucrose, maltose or lactose. The dependent variable is the mass of glucose produced after 10 minutes.

(b) Tube 4 is a negative control. It contains sucrose but no enzyme. Only 0.1 mg of glucose appeared in Tube 4, which shows that sucrose does not break down appreciably on its own in 10 minutes and that little glucose was present to begin with. Therefore the much larger amount of glucose in Tube 1 (4.8 mg) can be attributed to the activity of sucrase.

(c) Glucose due to the enzyme = 4.8 mg − 0.1 mg = 4.7 mg. Rate = 4.7 mg ÷ 10 min = 0.47 mg glucose per minute.

(d) For an enzyme-catalyzed reaction to occur, the shape and charge of the substrate must be compatible with the enzyme's active site. Sucrose fits the active site of sucrase and forms an enzyme-substrate complex, so it is hydrolyzed into glucose and fructose. Maltose and lactose have different shapes and charge distributions that are not compatible with the active site. They do not form an enzyme-substrate complex, are not hydrolyzed, and produce no more glucose than the no-enzyme control. Sucrase increases the rate of sucrose hydrolysis because, as a biological catalyst, it lowers the activation energy of the reaction, so more substrate molecules react per unit time.

item.title: Active-Site Charge and the Rate of an Enzyme Reaction
item.stimulus:
A bacterial enzyme, phosphatase P, removes a phosphate group from its substrate. The substrate carries a negative charge near the bond that is broken. In the wild-type enzyme, a lysine amino acid with a positively charged R group lines the active site. Researchers made a mutant version of the enzyme in which this lysine is replaced by glutamate, an amino acid with a negatively charged R group. Structural studies show that the mutant enzyme folds into the same overall three-dimensional shape as the wild-type enzyme.

The researchers set up three tubes. Each tube contained the same volume of buffer at pH 7 and the same substrate concentration, and all tubes were kept at 37 °C. Tube 1 received wild-type enzyme, tube 2 received an equal amount of mutant enzyme, and tube 3 received an equal volume of buffer with no enzyme. The amount of product formed in 10 minutes was measured.

Tube | Contents | Product formed in 10 min (µmol)
1 | Wild-type enzyme + substrate | 48.0
2 | Mutant enzyme + substrate | 6.0
3 | No enzyme + substrate | 0.2
item.model_answer:
(a) Phosphatase P is a protein that acts as a biological catalyst. It binds the substrate in its active site and lowers the activation energy of the reaction, so the reaction proceeds much faster than it would without the enzyme.

(b) The independent variable is the version of enzyme added to each tube (wild-type enzyme, mutant enzyme, or no enzyme). Tube 3 is a negative control: it shows how much product forms from the substrate on its own, without any enzyme (only 0.2 µmol). This baseline shows that the much larger amounts of product in tubes 1 and 2 are caused by enzyme activity rather than by spontaneous breakdown of the substrate.

(c) Wild-type rate = 48.0 µmol ÷ 10 min = 4.8 µmol/min. Mutant rate = 6.0 µmol ÷ 10 min = 0.6 µmol/min. Percent decrease = (4.8 − 0.6) ÷ 4.8 × 100 = 87.5%.

(d) For a reaction to occur, the shape and charge of the substrate must be compatible with the active site so an enzyme-substrate complex can form. In the wild type, the positively charged lysine R group attracts the negatively charged substrate and holds it in the active site. In the mutant, the negatively charged glutamate R group repels the negatively charged substrate. Even though the overall shape is unchanged, the charge mismatch means the substrate binds less often, so fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form and less product is made per minute.

item.title: Active Site Charge and Enzyme Catalysis Rate
item.stimulus:
Enzyme P is a protein that speeds up the removal of a phosphate group from substrate S. The phosphate group on S carries a negative charge. In the active site of normal (wild-type) enzyme P, the R group of a lysine amino acid is positively charged. This lysine binds the phosphate group of S when the enzyme-substrate complex forms.

Researchers produced a mutant version of enzyme P. In the mutant, this one lysine is replaced by glutamate, whose R group is negatively charged. Structural analysis showed that the mutant enzyme folds into the same overall three-dimensional shape as the wild-type enzyme.

The researchers set up three tubes. Each tube contained the same volume of buffer at pH 7.5 and 25°C, and the same concentration of substrate S. They then added one of the following: buffer only (no enzyme), wild-type enzyme P, or mutant enzyme P, using equal amounts of enzyme. After 10 minutes they measured the amount of free phosphate released.

Tube | Enzyme added | Phosphate released in 10 min (µmol)
1 | None (buffer only) | 0.2
2 | Wild-type enzyme P | 48.0
3 | Mutant enzyme P | 3.0
item.model_answer:
(a) Enzyme P is a biological catalyst. When S binds in its active site and forms an enzyme-substrate complex, the enzyme lowers the activation energy needed for the phosphate to be removed. With a lower energy barrier, the reaction happens much faster, so tube 2 released 48.0 µmol of phosphate compared with only 0.2 µmol in tube 1 without enzyme.

(b) The independent variable is the type of enzyme added to the tube: no enzyme, wild-type enzyme P, or mutant enzyme P. Tube 1 is a control because it measures how much phosphate is released from substrate S on its own, without any enzyme. Since tube 1 released only 0.2 µmol, the much larger amounts in tubes 2 and 3 can be attributed to the enzymes rather than to spontaneous breakdown of S or something in the buffer.

(c) For the reaction to occur, both the shape and the charge of the substrate must be compatible with the active site. In the wild-type enzyme the positively charged lysine attracts the negatively charged phosphate of S, holding the substrate in the active site. In the mutant, the glutamate R group is negatively charged, so it repels the negative phosphate group. Even though the shape is the same, the charge is no longer compatible, so S binds poorly and fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form. As a result, the mutant catalyzes much less phosphate removal (3.0 µmol versus 48.0 µmol).

item.title: Invertase Substrate Specificity and Reaction Rate
item.stimulus:
Invertase is an enzyme that hydrolyzes the disaccharide sucrose into glucose and fructose. Students set up four test tubes at 37°C. Each tube held 5 mL of pH 4.5 buffer plus the contents listed below. Solutions were the same volume and concentration in every tube. After 10 minutes, the students measured the mass of glucose in each tube with a glucose assay. Lactose is a disaccharide made of glucose and galactose, so any hydrolysis of lactose would also release glucose.

Tube | Contents | Glucose after 10 min (mg)
1 | sucrose + invertase | 4.8
2 | sucrose + buffer (no enzyme) | 0.1
3 | lactose + invertase | 0.1
4 | invertase + buffer (no sugar) | 0.0
item.model_answer:
(a) The independent variable is the type of substrate added (sucrose in tube 1, lactose in tube 3). The dependent variable is the mass of glucose produced after 10 minutes.

(b) Tube 2 contains sucrose but no invertase, so it shows how much glucose forms from sucrose on its own, through spontaneous hydrolysis or background glucose. Because tube 2 produced only 0.1 mg, the extra glucose in tube 1 can be attributed to invertase rather than to sucrose breaking down without the enzyme.

(c) Glucose due to the enzyme = 4.8 mg − 0.1 mg = 4.7 mg. Rate = 4.7 mg ÷ 10 min = 0.47 mg/min.

(d) Invertase is a protein catalyst that lowers the activation energy needed to hydrolyze sucrose. With a lower energy barrier, many more sucrose molecules react per minute, so tube 1 produced much more glucose than tube 2, where the uncatalyzed reaction is very slow. In tube 3, the shape and charge of lactose are not compatible with invertase's active site. Lactose cannot bind and form an enzyme-substrate complex, so it is not hydrolyzed. The glucose level stays at the same background level as the no-enzyme tube.

t1=4.8
t2=0.1
t3=0.1
time=10
corrected=t1-t2
assert abs(corrected-4.7)<1e-9
rate=corrected/time
assert abs(rate-0.47)<1e-9
assert abs(t3-t2)<1e-9
